You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say in Draconic, just above the trickle of the water: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long breath there is only water. Then a small shape unfolds from the dark of the tunnel, hooded and thin, with a mending-knife held low and steady in one hand. She stops three paces off. Her voice, when it comes, is rough with disuse and nearly steady.

"Say what I cut into your boots."

"A crescent with a notch. The winter you were six. You said it was so I'd never lose them." Your throat closes on the last word.

The knife drops. She shoves back the hood, and she has your father's jaw and your mother's eyes, a scar through one eyebrow, and a hard, tired face that is twenty years old and has been alone for most of them. She hits you in the chest with both fists, once, hard, and then holds on to your shirt and does not let go.

You hold her for a time that neither of you measures. The water goes on running.

When she can speak, it is quick and low, because the wall is above you. An old hermit-herder took her in after the raid, fed her, taught her the high rocks, and died two winters ago. She watched the cairn every season and left the goat. She heard that the Foreman keeps a ledger in the ledger-house at the third gate, naming every hand taken and the cell it is held in, and she came as a mender in the autumn to get at it. On midwinter's eve the Foreman opens it for the great tally, and the next shipment of children goes out the following dawn. She wants the ledger stolen or burned before then, and she cannot do it alone.

"Keep being the bought man," she says. "Be loud. On the eve, draw the stair guards down to you, and I'll do the rest."

Her eyes are wet and fierce. It is nearly eleven at night, with the wall above and Ruk's torch still swinging.

What does Korvash say?

time: 5 minutes later: Day 16, 10:33:36 PM

You pull on your boots, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum Dargan's three rising notes, then say it in Draconic, barely above the trickle of the water. "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long moment there is only water. Then a voice answers from the dark, low and dry and utterly unlike a child's. "Say the seventh goat."

Your throat closes, but the old words come. "The seventh goat is lame in the off foreleg and bites the shepherd. She comes home last, and she comes home."

A small shape steps out of the black of the tunnel and lets the hood fall back. She is lean and wiry and not much past your shoulder, red-scaled like you, with a nick in one horn and a mender's needle-case at her belt. Her eyes are your father's. They are fierce and wet at once, and they do not leave your face.

"You're loud," says Tessa. "You've always been loud. I heard you at the cairn from three ridges away." Her mouth shakes, and she bites it still. Then she crosses the rocks in three strides and hits you in the chest with both fists, once, hard, and holds on.

You hold her. Neither of you says anything for a long time. The water runs past your boots, and far above, a bell tolls the half hour.

When she pulls back, she wipes her face on her sleeve, all business again, and speaks fast and low. "We have until the third night bell before the wash-house door is checked. Listen. I did not come to Greyshaft to hide. I came for the ledger. The Foreman writes down every hand the Tallies ever took, by name and steading, and I have read it, Kor. Dargan's clan is in it. Not all dead." She grips your wrist. "There are names still marked *working*, in the deep galleries, and one of them is Aunt Orsa's boy. And the Foreman has a page for you that isn't the one he showed you. I've seen it."

Tessa has said more in a minute than in fourteen years. It is near ten thirty-five, and the culvert breathes cold on both of you. What does Korvash say?

She pushes back the hood. The scales along her brow are a darker red than yours, and one horn is chipped. Your father's jaw is plain on her face.

Then her composure cracks all at once and she crosses the gap in two strides and hits you in the chest with both fists, then holds on to your shirt and does not let go. You put your arms around her and feel how light she is.

Eleven children, the ones the Tallies took from the steadings this autumn who weren't in Gorrak's thirty-one. The Foreman means to ship them to the deep galleries at midwinter. That's why he wanted an axe on the walls by then." Her eyes are hard now. "I couldn't do it alone. I needed someone who'd come."

Far above, a lantern swings along the third gate's wall, and a voice calls a name that might be "Mender?" She stiffens and her hand goes to her knife.

It is half past ten, four days before midwinter's eve. You hold your sister, with a plan half spoken and a lantern coming down the stair. What does Korvash do?

Gorrak let me slip away twice and keeps his scouts off me, but he doesn't know what I know." Her hands close on your sleeve. "On midwinter's eve the Foreman sends the season's ledger and its 'hands' down the south road to a buyer. The ledger names every child the Tallies have taken, and some of them are still alive in the lower galleries, unsold. Kor, there are children down there from our own steadings."

She looks up at you, fierce and frightened and exactly her father's daughter. "I can get you into the ledger-house. I can't carry the ledger out alone, and I can't free them alone. But you can't know me. Not until it's done."

It is nearly eleven at night on day sixteen. Four days remain until midwinter's eve. What does Korvash say?

entries.text: notebook: updated Find Tessa
time: 30 minutes later: Day 16, 10:58:36 PM

You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, and then say it in Draconic, just above the trickle of water: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

Nothing moves. Then, from deep in the dark, a voice answers, low and hard and not a child's: "Say the seventh goat."

Your throat closes. You say it, the way Dargan sang it, the lost goat that comes home by the north gate with a bell on its neck. Then you add the line nobody outside the family would know, the one he made up for the two of you: "And the little one rides on the big one's back."

A figure steps out of the black. She is small, wiry, hooded, with a mender's awl held low in one fist like a knife. She stops at the edge of the starlight and pushes back the hood. Your father's jaw, your mother's brow, and a thin scar through one eyebrow you have never seen. She is nineteen now. She looks at you for a long time.

"You got big," Tessa says. Her voice breaks on the last word. Then she crosses the rocks in three strides and hits you in the chest with both fists, once, hard, and then holds on.

When she can speak again, it is fast and quiet. She hid in the rocks the night of the raid. A goat-keeper's widow took her in, and years later a slaver sold her into Greyshaft's tally under a false name. She has mended in the Foreman's ledger-house for two seasons, learning it. "The ledger records every child taken, who bought them, and where they went. Wren's page is in it, and thirty others. If it goes out of Greyshaft, it ends him. He reads the tally aloud on midwinter's eve, with his seal, before all the captains. I need you on the gallery door that night, loud and in his sight, and I need him looking at you."

She steps back, wipes her face with her wrist, and gives a crooked, furious smile. "Don't say you're sorry. Don't say anything. We've got four days. Nod if you're in."

It is nearly eleven, the wall above is quiet, and your sister is alive. What does Korvash say?

entries.text: notebook: updated Foreman's Scouts

You send the boy running and climb the rubble heap with the shield up and the sword out. Then you let the old loudness out, cracked and ragged, in Goblin and Common both, and it rolls up the gully like a rockfall. Two grey cloaks on a ridge. A whole camp's worth of you already past them. Dargan's son has walked ninety-four children out of the Foreman's mine, and anyone who wants his axe can come down and learn what it's worth.

It lands. The archer's bow sags a hand's breadth. The one with the sword looks at the length of the column, at the shale at your boots, and at the way you stand, and some tally goes through his head that comes out wrong for the Foreman. "We're paid in coin," he calls down, flat and a little hoarse. "Not in blood. Not for a ledger." He does not sheathe the sword, but he does not come down either.

Then, grudgingly, like a man paying off a debt to his own good sense, he adds: "You're late for one thing, Emberhide. Foreman sent a rider to the Tin Mask two days gone, right after he had your cairn story out of the cook. Wants his count and wants it in person. Your captain'll be at the third gate by dusk tomorrow, and the move is that same night." He spits. "Whatever you're going to do about it, do it before then."

The other scout is already gone, a grey shape slipping back over the ridge toward Greyshaft with the news that Dargan's son led them out. The sword-man watches you a moment longer, then follows. The ridge is empty.

The column goes on. It is a little after half past seven, the sun is clear of the peaks, and by the time the gully opens onto a stream and the high road, you are walking with legs that don't feel like yours. Ninna is counting. Tessa has dropped back to walk beside you, and she is looking at you the way Dargan used to look at a ewe that had come in lame.

You are at 2 hit points. The children are free and moving toward Harrowmere, three days off. The master ledger is still on the third gate, and Gorrak is coming to Greyshaft by tomorrow's dusk. What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Break the Foreman's Ledger

You set the boy down and he bolts for Tessa. Then you climb the rubble with the shield up and the sword out, and you bellow it all up the gully in Goblin and Common. It should have been magnificent. It isn't. Your voice cracks on "Dargan's son", the heap of slate shifts under your boot, and you have to catch yourself on the shield. Your chest is heaving, and the bandage at your side is dark and wet.

The scouts look at you for a long moment. The one with the sword laughs, a short dry bark, and says something low to his partner in Goblin. You catch "one" and "bleeding". They have counted you now, and they know what they're counting.

The swordsman turns and goes back along the ridge at a lope, toward Greyshaft, and he is not hurrying because he doesn't need to. He is carrying your name to the Foreman: Dargan's son, alone, wounded, walking the children out. The archer stays. He lays the arrow on the string, and the point drifts past you, along the gully, to the last of the column where Ninna's head is bobbing, counting.

He hasn't loosed yet. He is waiting for you to move, or for the column to bunch. Below you the children are filing out of the gully's mouth into the open slope, with Tessa at the head, and they will be exposed for several minutes more.

You are at 2 hit points on a heap of slate, thirty feet below an archer who is taking his time. What does Korvash do?

When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. I set the boy down, tell him "Run to Tessa, lad, and don't stop," and climb onto the rubble heap with the shield up and the sword out, so the scouts have to look at me and not the column. Then I bellow up the gully in Goblin and Common alike, as loud as my cracked voice will go: "Two grey cloaks on a ridge, and a whole camp's worth of me already past you! Come down and learn what a Tally's axe is worth, or go and tell your Foreman Dargan's son walked ninety-four children out of his mine!"

"Ninna, Tessa, keep them moving!"

You set the boy on his feet. "Run to Tessa, lad, and don't stop." He goes like a hare. Then you climb the rubble heap with the shield up and the sword out, and you let the old loudness out of you at last, in Goblin and in Common, so that it bounces off both walls of the gully and comes back twice as big.

It works better than it has any right to. Your voice is cracked and your knees are water, but the gully makes a giant of you. On the ridge the archer's bow dips. The swordsman looks down the track for the army of Emberhides you swear is already past them, and sees only the rubble, the shield, and a great red-scaled shape that has not blinked. A dragonborn who is that loud is either mad or not alone, and neither is worth dying for before breakfast.

They say nothing, which is its own answer. The swordsman jerks his chin. They back off the lip together, grey cloaks dropping out of sight, and a moment later you hear boots on loose stone going back toward Greyshaft, fast. They are carrying your name to the Foreman. By the sound of it, they are in no hurry to carry it back with you attached.

You stand on the rubble until the sound is gone, and then your legs remind you that you are at 2 hit points. Ahead, Tessa has halted the head of the column at a bend and is looking back at you. Ninna is counting again. It is about seven in the morning, the stream is below, and the high road beyond it leads to Harrowmere three days off. The scouts will return, and so will worse. You have no food but your pouch of goat meat and ten rations, and the children have eaten nothing.

You set the boy down and he bolts for Tessa without a backward look. Then you climb the heap of fallen slate with the shield high and the sword out, a ragged red-scaled shape against the grey, and you let the old loudness out of you at full cracked pitch, in Goblin and then in Common, so there is no word of it either scout can pretend not to understand.

The gully has swallowed them. All they can see is one wounded dragonborn who has just told them his name and that he has taken the mine's whole harvest.

They don't come down. The archer mutters something short and sharp, and goes back over the ridge at a run toward Greyshaft, and you know exactly what he is running to say. The swordsman stays, a grey shape on the skyline, no longer hiding. He will shadow you now, and he is waiting for friends.

Behind you the column is moving. Ninna's whisper carries up the gully, "Keep going, hands on shoulders." Your legs have started to shake. You are at 2 hit points, it is nearly seven in the morning, and the Foreman knows whose son walked ninety-four children out of his mine.

It is just before seven in the morning. What does Korvash do?
